full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. YYY, ZZZ (ACQUITTED), AND XXX, ACCUSED; XXX, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: IV. Special Penal Laws > P. Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act (RA 9208, Secs. 3–6 and 10–12, as amended by RA 10364, 11862, and 12312)
topics: Elements of trafficking in persons under Sec. 4(a), RA 9208, as amended
Mere receipt or hiring of a person for exploitation, with or without consent
Liability of a non-owner bar manager; registered ownership neither required nor sufficient
Means: taking advantage of the vulnerability of a minor
Qualified trafficking when the victim is a child (Sec. 6(a))
doctrine:
Trafficking in persons under **Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364**, has three elements (reiterating *People v. Casio*): (1) the **act**: recruitment, obtaining, hiring, providing, offering, transportation, transfer, maintaining, harboring, or receipt of persons, "with or without the victim's consent or knowledge"; (2) the **means**: threat, force or other coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power or position, taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person, or giving or receiving payments or benefits to achieve the consent of one having control over another; and (3) the **purpose**: exploitation or prostitution of others, other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labor, slavery, servitude, or removal or sale of organs. The crime is **qualified under Section 6(a)** when the trafficked person is a child.

**The law punishes the mere receipt of persons for the purpose of trafficking, regardless of the victim's consent or knowledge.** A bar manager who hired and supervised a minor is liable even if she is not the owner of the bar and even if others brought the minor to her. Acts of trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of the establishment, and registered ownership by itself does not create criminal liability (*People v. Villanueva*). The means element is met by **taking advantage of the victim's vulnerability as a minor** (*People v. De Dios*), so the minor's admission that she was not forced to work and could have refused does not defeat the charge. Allowing customers to take the minor out for sex and collecting the "bar fine" establishes the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation.
facts:
XXX, YYY, and ZZZ were charged with qualified trafficking in persons. The Information alleged that on or about July 1, 2014 and for some time after, in a municipality in Isabela, they conspired to recruit, transport, hire, receive, keep, and maintain AAA, a 17-year-old minor, for prostitution and sexual exploitation, under the pretext of employing her as a guest relations officer (GRO) at a bar.

The prosecution showed that on July 1, 2014, AAA's friends BJE and ZZZ brought her to the bar, where she was introduced to XXX, who hired her as a GRO. XXX made her sit and drink with male customers ("pa-table") for a PHP 50.00 commission per bottle. XXX also let customers take AAA to a hotel for sex after they paid XXX a "bar fine." AAA testified that a customer told XXX he would take her out, and XXX only told him to return her. The customer had sex with her at a hotel and handed PHP 1,500.00 to XXX. AAA received no salary because the manager kept her commissions. She identified XXX as the one who "employed" and "hired" her. XXX herself testified that YYY told her AAA would work with her at the bar. Police rescued AAA on July 7, 2014; SPO2 Rañeses testified that AAA pointed to XXX as the manager. On cross-examination, AAA agreed that she was not forced to work at the bar and could say no if she did not want to work there.

XXX denied being the owner, manager, or supervisor, claiming she was only a GRO and that AAA's decision to go out with customers was her own. In its Decision dated December 8, 2017 (Criminal Case No. 23-2530), the RTC convicted XXX and YYY of qualified trafficking. It sentenced each to life imprisonment and a PHP 2 million fine and ordered them to pay solidarily PHP 500,000.00 moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 exemplary damages with interest; ZZZ was acquitted. YYY's appeal was dismissed for failure to file a brief. In its Decision dated July 2, 2020 (CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 10297), the CA affirmed XXX's conviction, modifying the interest to 6% per annum from finality.
issues: Whether XXX performed the act of trafficking (hiring or receiving AAA) even though she was allegedly not the owner of the bar and others brought AAA to her.
Whether the element of means was proved despite AAA's admission that she was not forced to work at the bar.
Whether the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation was proved, so as to sustain XXX's conviction for qualified trafficking in persons.
ruling:
**1. Yes, XXX hired or received AAA.** AAA testified that XXX "employed" and "hired" her. XXX herself admitted that YYY brought AAA and told her that AAA would work with her at the bar, and SPO2 Rañeses testified that AAA pointed to XXX as the manager. Even assuming XXX was not the registered owner, she is no less guilty. *People v. Villanueva* held that being the registered owner per se does not make one criminally liable, and the acts of trafficking "may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of establishments." **"The law punishes the mere receipt of persons, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for purpose of trafficking."** XXX was responsible for hiring and supervising AAA.

**2. Yes, the means element was proved.** AAA agreed on cross-examination that she was not forced to work at the bar and could say no. But under *People v. De Dios*, trafficking may be committed by **taking advantage of the person's vulnerability as a minor**, as here. The element was further achieved through the financial gain from the illicit services AAA provided to customers.

**3. Yes, the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation was proved.** XXX made AAA sit with customers. A customer spoke to XXX before taking AAA to a hotel, and XXX told him to return her afterward. The customer handed the PHP 1,500.00 "bar fine" to XXX, who kept AAA's commissions. These facts belie XXX's claim that she never pimped AAA and had nothing to do with AAA's decision to go out with customers. **Since AAA was 17, the trafficking is qualified under Section 6(a).**
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED, and the CA Decision dated July 2, 2020 in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 10297 was AFFIRMED. XXX was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of qualified trafficking in persons and sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine of PHP 2 million. She was ordered to pay the victim PHP 500,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 100,000.00 as exemplary damages, both earning legal interest of 6% per annum from finality until fully paid.

bar_questions.q: Rina manages a videoke bar owned by her cousin. Two friends of Lea, a 16-year-old, brought Lea to the bar looking for work, and Rina took her in as a "waitress." Rina had Lea sit and drink with male customers, and allowed customers to take Lea to a motel for sex after they paid Rina a "bar fine," which Rina kept. Charged with qualified trafficking in persons, Rina argues that (1) she is not the owner of the bar, (2) she did not recruit Lea, since Lea's friends brought her, and (3) Lea agreed to work there. Decide.

alac.answer: Rina is guilty of qualified trafficking in persons. None of her defenses is valid.
alac.legal_basis: Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364, punishes the recruitment, hiring, maintaining, or receipt of a person, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for the purpose of prostitution or sexual exploitation. The means element includes taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person. Under Section 6(a), trafficking is qualified when the trafficked person is a child. "The law punishes the mere receipt of persons, with or without the victim's consent or knowledge, for purpose of trafficking," and the acts of trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners of the establishment. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025)
alac.application: (1) Ownership is not an element; Rina personally performed the acts of trafficking as the one who took in and supervised Lea. (2) Even if Lea's friends brought her, Rina hired and received her, and the mere receipt of a person for exploitation is punished. (3) Lea's consent is immaterial: the law punishes the act with or without the victim's consent. The means element is supplied by taking advantage of Lea's vulnerability as a minor and by the financial gain from her services. The purpose of prostitution is shown by Rina's practice of letting customers take Lea out for sex upon payment of a bar fine that Rina kept. Lea is 16, so the crime is qualified.
alac.conclusion: Rina is liable for qualified trafficking in persons under Section 4(a) in relation to Section 6(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended.

bar_questions.q: Tony is the registered owner of a bar where a 17-year-old was found working as a GRO and being sent out with customers for sex. The evidence shows that Tony lives abroad, that the bar was run entirely by its manager, and that there is no proof that Tony hired, received, or dealt with the minor or knew of her exploitation. May Tony be convicted of qualified trafficking in persons solely because he is the registered owner of the bar?

alac.answer: No. Registered ownership of the establishment does not by itself make Tony criminally liable for trafficking.
alac.legal_basis: Being the registered owner of an establishment per se does not make one criminally liable for the acts of trafficking committed there; the acts constituting trafficking may be performed by persons who may or may not be registered owners. Liability attaches to whoever performs the punishable acts (recruitment, hiring, maintaining, receipt, and the like) for the purpose of exploitation. (People v. XXX, G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025, citing People v. Villanueva)
alac.application: Liability for trafficking depends on performing the acts in Section 4(a) for an exploitative purpose, not on ownership. In People v. XXX, the manager was convicted though she was not the owner, because she hired and supervised the minor. The reverse also holds: Tony did not hire, receive, or maintain the minor, and nothing links him to her exploitation. The person liable is the manager who performed the acts.
alac.conclusion: Tony cannot be convicted of qualified trafficking based solely on his registered ownership of the bar.

bar_questions.q: Mon hired Lito, 19, as a "helper" in his club and made him provide sexual services to customers, collecting the fees himself. Lito has a moderate intellectual disability that leaves him unable to fully protect himself from abuse or exploitation. On cross-examination, Lito said nobody forced him to work at the club. (a) Does Lito's statement that he was not forced defeat the charge of trafficking? (b) Is the trafficking qualified even though Lito is already 19?

alac.answer: (a) No. The means element may be established by taking advantage of the victim's vulnerability, and the act of trafficking is punished with or without the victim's consent. (b) Yes. Under RA No. 9208, as amended, a "child" includes a person over 18 who cannot fully take care of or protect himself because of a physical or mental disability or condition, so the trafficking is qualified.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 4(a) of RA No. 9208, as amended by RA No. 10364, the act of trafficking is punished "with or without the victim's consent or knowledge." The means include "taking advantage of the vulnerability of the person." In People v. XXX (G.R. No. 264132, August 13, 2025), the minor's admission that she was not forced to work did not defeat the charge, because the means element was met by taking advantage of her vulnerability as a minor and by the financial gain from her services. Section 6(a) qualifies trafficking when the trafficked person is a child. Section 3(b), as amended, as quoted in the decision, defines a child as "a person below [18] years of age or one who is over [18] but is unable to fully take care of or protect himself/herself from abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, or discrimination because of a physical or mental disability or condition."
alac.application: (a) Lito's statement that nobody forced him addresses only force. Mon took advantage of Lito's vulnerability arising from his intellectual disability and profited from his sexual services, which satisfies the means element. Consent does not matter to the act element. (b) Lito is 19, but his disability leaves him unable to fully protect himself from exploitation, so he falls within the statutory definition of a child. The trafficking is therefore qualified under Section 6(a).
alac.conclusion: Lito's lack of complaint about force is no defense, and Mon is liable for qualified trafficking in persons.

notes: Many anonymized "People v. XXX" cases exist; cite this one with its G.R. No. 264132. Co-accused YYY's appeal before the CA was dismissed for failure to file a brief, and ZZZ was acquitted by the RTC; neither was before the Supreme Court. The RTC had imposed 12% interest from April 28, 2015; the CA changed it to 6% from finality, which the Court affirmed. The definition of "child" in Bar Question 3 is from footnote 15 of the decision (RA No. 9208, Sec. 3(b), as amended); the Court did not apply that clause in this case, since AAA was 17.
